sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, match the columns, true/false or a short passage).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks (any two): (a) A close interaction between organisms of different species is ________. (b) The death rate of a population is called ________. (c) Conversion of ammonia into nitrates is ________. (d) Interconnected food chains form a ________.
Write True (T) or False (F) (any two): (a) Fish and prawns have gills. (b) Penguins have a hump to store fat. (c) Population growth curves are J- or S-shaped. (d) Abiotic components are organisms.

Fill in the blanks: (a) The ________ cycle is the biogeochemical cycle by which carbon is exchanged among living things, water and air. (b) Dead organisms return nitrogen to the soil as ________ compounds.

Read the passage about a pond ecosystem and answer: (a) What will happen to the nutrients if there are no decomposers? (b) Which abiotic factor caused the faster growth of algae after a few sunny days?
questions.answer: (a) Nutrients will not be recycled; dead matter will pile up and nutrients will stay locked in it. (b) Sunlight.

questions.q: Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Birds have hollow bones to make them heavier. (b) Camels store fat in their humps.
questions.answer: (a) False — hollow bones make them lighter. (b) True

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Bats have an extension of ________ between the fingers of the forelimbs that helps them fly; the biggest source of nitrogen is ________.

sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: In this grassland the producer is —
The frog is a —
The feeding links of grass, rabbits, grasshoppers, frogs, snakes and hawks together form a —
If grass has 10,000 J of energy, the energy reaching the frog will be about —
Bacteria and fungi in this ecosystem are —

sections.passage: In a grassland, grasshoppers feed on grass, frogs eat grasshoppers, snakes eat frogs and hawks eat snakes. Rabbits also eat grass and are eaten by hawks. When plants and animals die, bacteria and fungi break down their bodies. Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next level.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Write two differences between grazing and detritus food chains.
questions.answer: A grazing food chain starts with living green plants, eaten by herbivores (grass → deer → lion); a detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter broken down by decomposers (dead leaves → bacteria/fungi → earthworm → bird). The grazing chain passes energy captured by photosynthesis; the detritus chain recycles nutrients from dead matter.

or.q: Write a grazing food chain with an example.
or.answer: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk (in water: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish).

questions.q: Write two adaptations of desert animals that reduce water loss.
questions.answer: Any two: they excrete solid uric acid or concentrated urine; they have scaly, waterproof skin; they stay in burrows during the hot day and come out at night.

questions.q: Why is energy less at higher trophic levels?
questions.answer: At each level most of the energy taken in is used for life processes (respiration, movement) or lost as heat; only about 10% becomes body mass and passes to the next level.

questions.q: Why are detritus food chains important?
questions.answer: They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil, so nutrients are recycled and the environment is kept clean.

or.q: Give two ways to replenish forests.
or.answer: Afforestation/reforestation (planting trees where forests are cut) and social forestry or banning illegal felling and protecting forests from fire and grazing.

questions.q: Name two adaptations of the lotus to live in water.
questions.answer: Long, spongy stem with air spaces that keeps it afloat and bends with currents; broad floating leaves with a waxy upper surface and stomata on the upper side.

questions.q: Differentiate between emigration and immigration and state their effect on population size.
questions.answer: Emigration is permanent movement of individuals out of a population — it decreases the population. Immigration is permanent movement into a population — it increases it.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: What are mesophytes? Write two structural features.
questions.answer: Mesophytes are land plants that grow where water is neither very scarce nor in excess. Features: large, thin, broad leaves with many stomata on the lower surface; well-developed, branched roots with root caps; well-organised shoot system.

questions.q: Draw a labelled diagram of energy flow through the trophic levels of an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Diagram: Sun → producers (trophic level I) → herbivores (II) → carnivores (III) → top carnivores (IV), as boxes that become smaller upward, with arrows passing energy upward and arrows at each level showing energy lost as heat (respiration); decomposers receive energy from every level. Energy flow is one-way and decreases at each level.
questions.note: April 2017 asked: energy flow in a food chain and why energy decreases up the chain.

questions.q: What is symbiosis? Give an example. How is commensalism different from symbiosis (mutualism)?
questions.answer: Symbiosis is the close living together of two organisms of different species, e.g. alga and fungus in lichen, or bees and flowers. In mutualism both partners benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (sucker fish on a shark).

questions.q: What is population dispersal? Describe its two types.
questions.answer: Dispersal is the movement of individuals into or out of an area, which changes the size of the population. Emigration is permanent movement out of a population (decreases it); immigration is permanent movement into a population (increases it).

questions.q: Name two types of food chains and give two significances of food chains and food webs.
questions.answer: Grazing food chain (starts with green plants) and detritus food chain (starts with dead organic matter). Significance: they maintain ecological balance; they show feeding relationships; energy flows and nutrients cycle through them.

questions.q: What is adaptation? Write three adaptations of birds for flight.
questions.answer: Adaptation is a special feature that helps an organism live in its habitat. Birds: streamlined body; forelimbs modified into feathered wings; hollow, light bones; strong flight muscles.

questions.q: Write four adaptations of desert plants.
questions.answer: Succulent stems or leaves that store water (cactus); leaves reduced to spines to cut transpiration; few, sunken stomata and thick waxy cuticle; deep, widespread roots to absorb maximum water.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Draw a schematic diagram of the nitrogen cycle and explain the process.
questions.answer: Diagram: atmospheric N₂ → (lightning; nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules and soil) → nitrates in soil → absorbed by plants (proteins) → eaten by animals → excreta and dead bodies → ammonia (ammonifying bacteria) → nitrites and nitrates (nitrifying bacteria) → back to plants, or → N₂ (denitrifying bacteria). Steps: (1) nitrogen fixation by lightning and by microbes such as Rhizobium and blue-green algae; (2) assimilation of nitrates by plants into amino acids and proteins, passed to animals; (3) ammonification of urea, excreta and dead matter into ammonia; (4) nitrification — Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter convert ammonia into nitrites and nitrates; (5) denitrification — Pseudomonas returns nitrogen gas to the air.
questions.note: April 2021 asked for two ways of fixing atmospheric nitrogen and the difference between nitrogen assimilation and ammonification.

questions.q: What is an ecosystem? Describe the abiotic and biotic components of a pond.
questions.answer: An ecosystem is a unit of all the living organisms of an area together with their non-living surroundings, interacting with each other. Pond — abiotic: water, sunlight, temperature, dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide, minerals, soil and stones at the bottom. Biotic: producers — phytoplankton, algae and rooted or floating plants such as Hydrilla and lotus; consumers — zooplankton and insect larvae (primary), small fish and frogs (secondary), large fish and birds (tertiary); decomposers — bacteria and fungi in the mud that break down dead matter.

questions.q: Describe the role of adaptations with examples: (a) spongy stem of lotus (b) desert reptiles excrete uric acid (c) thick feathers of penguins (d) eyes on top of the head in aquatic animals. Also explain detritus and grazing food chains.
questions.answer: (a) Air spaces make the stem light and buoyant and it bends with currents. (b) Uric acid is excreted as a near-solid, saving water in the desert. (c) Densely packed feathers trap air and reduce heat loss in extreme cold. (d) The animal can stay hidden under water while watching for predators or prey above. Grazing chain: starts with green plants (grass → deer → tiger). Detritus chain: starts with dead organic matter (dead leaves → bacteria → earthworm → bird).

questions.q: Compare the S-shaped and J-shaped population growth curves.
questions.answer: S-shaped (sigmoid): growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid (growth phase, births far exceed deaths), then levels off at the carrying capacity (stable phase) as environmental resistance makes births equal deaths. J-shaped: the population grows exponentially until environmental resistance suddenly takes effect, and then crashes as deaths rise sharply. The S curve shows gradual regulation; the J curve shows sudden collapse.
